transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in, and what concerns have you been dealing with lately?

Hello. I work as a healthcare operations manager, and lately, during long meetings or when I’m working through complex plans, my mind keeps drifting off and I miss important details even though I’m really trying to pay attention. It's starting to make me feel less on top of things at work, which is why I wanted to speak with you today.

Have these attention problems been present since childhood or earlier in life, or did they start more recently during a stressful period or after a specific life change? Do they happen in many settings, like at home too, or mainly at work?

They actually go back to childhood—my elementary teachers always said I was bright but daydreamed and lost homework, though it's gotten much worse over the last two years with my increased responsibilities. It definitely happens outside of work too, like forgetting to pay bills, return calls, or attend community meetings unless I write them down immediately.

Along with the inattention, have you also had symptoms of hyperactivity or impulsivity since childhood—like feeling constantly restless, fidgeting, talking excessively, interrupting others, or acting before thinking? Or has it mainly been problems with attention and forgetfulness?

Since childhood, it has mainly been about the attention issues and forgetfulness, like my daydreaming and losing schoolwork. I don't really experience physical restlessness or fidgeting, but in adulthood, I do sometimes struggle with talking excessively and dominating conversations when I get excited about a project.

When you were a child, besides daydreaming and losing things, did you often interrupt others, blurt out answers, have trouble waiting your turn, or act without thinking? Or were those kinds of impulsive behaviors mostly absent back then?

Those kinds of impulsive behaviors were pretty much absent when I was a kid. Back then, my struggles were almost entirely focused on daydreaming, losing worksheets, and forgetting to turn in homework. My teachers and parents always noted how distracted and forgetful I was, rather than hyperactive or impulsive.
Before age 12, did these attention problems clearly cause problems in at least two settings, such as both school and home? Can you give one example from each?

Yes, they definitely did. At school, my teachers wrote on my report cards that I was bright but always daydreaming, losing worksheets, and forgetting to turn in homework I'd actually completed. At home, I was so forgetful that my parents always joked I would forget my head if it wasn't attached to my neck.

Do these attention problems currently cause clear impairment in at least two areas of your life, such as work, home, relationships, finances, or driving? What are the main problems they create day to day?

Yes, they definitely do. At work, my missed details have led to coworkers quietly double-checking my reports and taking over parts of projects, which has made me turn down new leadership opportunities. In my personal and community life, I constantly forget to pay bills, return calls, or attend board meetings, even though my phone is full of half-written reminder notes.

Have there been times when your attention got much worse only during periods of depression, anxiety, poor sleep, or increased alcohol/cannabis use? Or has this pattern been fairly constant across your life regardless of those factors?

This pattern has been fairly constant throughout my life and isn't tied to periods of depression, anxiety, or substance use. It dates all the way back to my childhood, though it has become much more of a struggle over the last couple of years simply because my workload and responsibilities have expanded so much.

opening_question.question: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in, and what concerns have you been dealing with lately?

final_diagnosis.reason: Lifelong, cross-situational inattention beginning in childhood with clear evidence before age 12 in both school and home, and current impairment in multiple domains. Hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms are largely absent, supporting predominantly inattentive ADHD rather than another condition. Symptoms are described as persistent and not limited to depression, anxiety, sleep problems, or substance use.
